Jet 2 Holiday · Prototype Phase 1 & 2 · CZ-01 + CZ-03

You cannot predict the morning a fare gets cheap.
You can predict the morning it gets expensive.

Checking a fare every day feels like doing something. Over 60 days of real Expedia searches it is mostly noise — until a few specific mornings, which arrive on a schedule the airline already published.

Cynthia Zhou · Expedia Flight Prices (one-way fares searched 16 Apr – 5 Oct 2022)

78%
of mornings the fare barely moved (under 10% either way)
12%
of mornings it rose 10% or more
10%
of mornings it fell 10% or more
51%
rose 10%+ on the worst single morning (Labor Day, 5 days out, just past the 7-day cutoff)

Based on 11,318,332 same-flight day-over-day price checks.

What the two views are doing

CZ-01, the diary (top) is the hook. Each row is one flight that was really searchable every morning for about two months; each cell is one of those mornings, coloured only by whether the lowest fare moved 10% or more. The field is almost entirely grey. That is the finding: a traveller refreshing a fare has, on most days, nothing to react to.

CZ-03, the staircase (bottom) is the answer. Pooling the same flights into a median shows the structure the diary hides: the fare holds roughly flat, bottoms out, and then steps up — and the steps land next to the 21-, 14- and 7-day advance-purchase cutoffs, which is why the same mornings light up red across unrelated routes.

The link between them is the point of putting them together. Clicking a diary row draws that one flight's own fare path on top of the median, with its dots carrying the diary's red/blue/grey coding. You get to see a single traveller's experience and the population pattern on one pair of axes: the individual path is jagged and unhelpful, the median is a staircase, and both are the same data.

Built in Python with Altair; rendered as Vega-Lite 6 in the browser. Clean data: data/cz_diary.csv, data/cz_staircase.csv, data/cz_changes.csv — exported by src/kaggle_export.py from the Kaggle dataset dilwong/flightprices. Fares are the lowest total fare per flight per search day; a change is measured against the same flight's previous search within 3 days.
